newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bond market still betting on reduced supply.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bond market still betting on reduced supply.

text.p: The long end of the U.S. bond market should be bolstered by expectations of reduced supply following an expected eventual Treasury elimination of one of its issues, analysts said.

"What matters most (for the 30-year bond) are underlying economic fundamentals and inflation," said Brian Wesbury, chief economist at Griffin, Kubik, Stephens & Thompson Inc. "But (less supply) will help the tone in the market. It could help psychology."

Many market participants were betting that when the Treasury announces details of next week's quarterly refunding on Wednesday, it would say August's 30-year bond offering would be the last one for the year.
"That's been driving the flattening trade," said Vincent Verterano, head trader at Nomura Securities.
Indeed, the spread between the 30-year and two-year has narrowed to 59 basis points from 67 basis points three weeks ago, and from above 70 just before the July 4 holiday.

At the same time, the 30-year to 10-year spread narrowed to 28 basis points from above 30 basis points, and analysts said they expected that spread to tighten further in upcoming weeks as flows from mortgage backed securities into 10-year notes wane.

On Monday, when the Treasury said it was not cutting its November 30-year bond issue, bond prices sagged -- but only briefly, until Treasury announced that it needed to borrow only $10 billion in the third quarter, half of what was anticipated.
So, even if there will be a 30-year offering in November, players figure the Treasury will cut the sizes and/or eliminate some monthly five-year note auctions, which would also help the market.

Further, some reasoned, eliminating a 30-year this year, even with significant progress on the budget deficit front, would have been too radical, since Treasury just recently eliminated two regular 10-year auctions.
And besides, the Treasury last year added a third bond sale, after moving to two 30-year auctions from four in 1994.

All, however, is dependent on the budget deficit outlook, analysts noted. The deficit is forecast at around $40 billion in fiscal 1997, but predictions for 1998 range from a $10 billion surplus to a $50 billion deficit.

It remains unclear to the market what Tuesday's budget pact between the Democratic White House and Republican Congressional leaders -- which included $90 billion in tax cuts, a $500 per child tax credit and changes in Medicare -- would do to the budget deficit.

The continued fall in the defict has surprised just about everyone, given how much the amazing strength in the economy and the surge in the stock market have contributed to higher than expected tax receipts.
Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp, said that the budget pact could widen the deficit more, which is why the Treasury did not cut the November bond issue.
(But) "In the next year-and-a-half," he said, "they will get rid of (auction)," he said.
